strengths: Well-motivated problem with compelling evidence (30% conflicts in UltraFeedback) for why fine-grained preferences are needed but introduce challenges
Solid theoretical contributions: sound DMPO derivation, rigorous loss bound analysis (Theorems 3.6-3.7), and elegant exchange argument proving optimality of high-consensus selection
Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple metrics (AlpacaEval 2, length-controlled scores, pairwise evaluation on 5 datasets) and systematically controlled conflict levels
Strong and consistent empirical results: >10% relative improvement over oracle baseline while using only 30% of training data, across all conflict levels
Thoughtful practical implementation with clever cross-pseudo reward estimation for PD term and explicit length bias mitigation through both sampling strategy and loss penalty
Clear presentation with good intuitive explanations of the PD term's role as implicit sample weighting mechanism
Enables a new practical paradigm where fine-grained preference collection + data selection replaces infeasible holistic annotation
weaknesses: Significant theory-practice gap: theorem assumes known φk but practice requires error-prone pseudo-reward estimation; effects of estimation errors on loss bounds not analyzed
Theorem 3.7's 'mild condition' (2(κ-1)/κ·r ≤ c2-c0) not verified empirically; restrictiveness and practical implications unclear
Limited experimental scope: evaluation only on UltraFeedback variants with fixed 4 aspects; lacks validation on diverse datasets with different aspect counts or types

PD estimation uses non-standard 'all-in-one' model with system prompts trained on 30% of data; design choice not well justified compared to separate reward models; quantile normalization removes theoretical interpretability
Core selection principle (prioritizing high-consensus samples) is relatively intuitive once PD term identified; novelty somewhat incremental over identifying the PD term itself
Incomplete baseline comparisons: missing recent data selection methods for preference optimization; Oracle baseline requiring 4x annotation effort is somewhat unrealistic
Computational overhead substantial (52.2 GPU hours total vs 33.6 for baseline); scalability concerns for scenarios with many aspects (κ >> 4)
Notation and definitions could be clearer: c0, c1, c2 introduced without clear motivation; Definition 3.3 assumes non-existent ground-truth holistic reward
